question: to the Commission Sandra Kalniete (PPE) Subject:

A campaign is being carried out in Latvia inviting residents to enter into agreements concerning the recovery of allegedly unlawful State aid. The organisers of the campaign claim that the European Commission, in its 2017 decision in Case SA.43140, declared the aid to be ‘unlawful’ because Latvia had infringed Article 108(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU). Although Latvia introduced the aid prior to the Commission’s final decision, in its decision the Commission declared the aid to be compatible with the internal market pursuant to Article 107(3)(c) TFEU, and raised no objections. Similar conclusions were also reached in the Commission’s 2020 decision (SA.56310). As Latvia’s competent authorities explain, aid that is declared ‘unlawful’ (because not notified in time) but compatible with the internal market does not give rise to an obligation for the Member State to recover it. In order to provide comprehensive information to the Latvian public, could the Commission clarify the following: 1.

Does the infringement of Article 108(3) TFEU identified in the Commission’s 2017 and 2020 decisions entitle electricity consumers –businesses and households – to request the recovery of the State aid paid?

Under EU legislation and in light of the above-mentioned decisions, does Latvia have a legal duty to recover payments from aid recipients, even though the aid was declared compatible with the internal market?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) 1. Where national law grants consumers (private persons or companies) standing, they can bring an action before the competent national courts in relation to unlawful aid, including asking to order its recovery. Under EU law, if aid is later approved, it does not have to be paid back. However, interest must still be paid for the time the aid was unlawful, to remove any unfair advantage obligation (Article 108(3) Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union). This interest is paid to the State budget, not to consumers. Consumers may still seek compensation separately under national law. 2. Under EU law, national authorities and courts must remove any unfair advantage gained from unlawful aid. In practice, this means beneficiaries must pay interest for the period during which they wrongly had access to the aid. The exact amount of interest is calculated under national law by the Member State concerned and the Member State must quantify the exact amount of interest to be recovered.
